description: I'm currently a y2 computer engineering student in NTU.Trying to do my first hackathon.
summary: Sol by Sol is a free browser game for kids aged 7 to 12. Players run a small base in Jezero crater on Mars for 15 sols until the return rocket launches. Every sol they walk across a real NASA orbital photo to explore, repair and build, then share a limited amount of power between life support, oxygen, a greenhouse and a radiation shield. Solar storms, dust storms and failing parts are hidden: the only way to see them coming is to call Earth, which costs an action point today. The two solar storms in each mission are real coronal mass ejections from NASA's DONKI database. Every choice costs something, and when a mission fails, the debrief explains why using the player's own numbers. It answers the challenge by letting young learners feel real mission trade-offs instead of reading about them.
details:
What it does: Sol by Sol turns mission planning into a game a child can feel. Each sol has four phases. In the morning report the player reads what the crew knows: today's weather, Mission Control's orders and any reply from Earth. In the daytime the player walks an astronaut across a real Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter photo of Jezero crater with three action points: collect samples at 11 survey sites in six regions, check and clean the solar panels, tend the greenhouse, repair a worn part, build equipment, or call Earth. At night the player shares the day's power between life support, the oxygen maker, the greenhouse and the shield room, with a live preview of tomorrow. The night report explains why every number changed and which real solar storm hit.

Real trade-offs, no free choices: The shield room protects the crew from a solar storm but takes power that could make oxygen. Far sites give more research but cost battery, air and radiation dose, and radiation never goes down. Calling Earth costs an action point and the answer only arrives the next morning, because radio takes minutes each way, but Earth's spacecraft are the only ones that can see a storm coming. Research unlocks eight NASA-inspired blueprints (a drill, rope, a scout helicopter, a pressurised rover, a better oxygen maker and more) that the crew must build with action points and power.

Made for young players: Pip the robot guide says one useful sentence at a time. Supplies are big rings with faces instead of bare numbers. Knowledge cards are one sentence long, with the full sourced text behind "Learn more". A bouncing arrow guides the first sol, and a failed mission ends with a debrief built from the player's own run, so failure teaches instead of punishing. The game runs in any browser on computers and phones, with no download or account, in English and Chinese.

Look and sound: Cartoon drawings of the base, sites and rover stand on the real orbital photo (labelled as AI-generated in the game). A small jazz combo, synthesized live in the browser, follows the game, and the real wind, laser and driving sounds recorded by NASA's Perseverance rover play as ambience.

Tested balance: Bot players played 600 missions per play style. Doing nothing never wins, rushing to far sites wins 11%, following orders 46%, also calling Earth 74%, and planning ahead 83%. The biggest single jump comes from calling Earth: exactly the habit real crews depend on.

Tools: Plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript with no framework and no build step, hosted on GitHub Pages. All game rules live in one seeded, testable module, and every number is anchored to a real-world fact noted in the code. Code and documentation: https://github.com/zhangxiaozhuang398-max/sol-by-sol

What is next: A classroom mode where a whole class plays the same mission and compares choices; the same rules at an Artemis-style outpost on the Moon; and an optional live mode that reads today's space weather alerts. Team Cainong: Zhang Xiaozhuang and Liu Dong, Singapore.
